---
title: "Quiz: rectangle features"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

---

**Q1.** A two-rectangle feature (left − right) is placed on a flat region of grey level 120. What is its response? And on a region that is 120 on the left and 80 on the right, with rectangles of $10 \times 10$ pixels?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Flat: $100 \cdot 120 - 100 \cdot 120 = 0$. Edge: $100 \cdot 120 - 100 \cdot 80 = 4000$ (a mean difference of 40 grey levels).
:::

---

**Q2.** Two rectangle sums cost 4 lookups each. Why does the two-rectangle feature need only 6?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The two rectangles share a side, so two of their corners are the same table entries. Their coefficients are added (giving $\pm 2$) and each shared entry is read once: $8 - 2 = 6$.
:::

---

**Q3.** Which template would you use to find (a) a thin bright vertical line, (b) a horizontal edge, (c) a round dark spot of about 10 pixels?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
(a) The three-rectangle line template across, with the centre rectangle about as wide as the line (positive response). (b) The two-rectangle edge template top − bottom. (c) Centre − surround with a centre box of about 10 pixels: a strongly **negative** response (the centre is darker than its surroundings).
:::

---

**Q4.** Why is the feature response divided by the standard deviation of the detection window?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
To remove the effect of contrast (lighting, camera gain): with twice the contrast every difference doubles, and so does the SD. Dividing makes the response the same. A brightness offset needs no correction, because the weights of every template sum to zero.
:::

---

**Q5.** A $24 \times 24$ window holds about 160 000 rectangle features but only 576 pixels. Is the feature set a basis? Does that matter for detection?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No: the features are far more numerous than the pixels, so they are linearly dependent (overcomplete), and the image cannot be uniquely rebuilt from them in a stable way. For detection that does not matter: the aim is to **discriminate** faces from background, not to reconstruct. The redundancy offers many candidate features; learning picks the useful few.
:::

---

**Q6.** How do the 2D Haar wavelets differ from Haar-like features?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Haar wavelets use only dyadic sizes (powers of two) at fixed grid positions and form an orthonormal basis (the transform is invertible, useful for compression). Haar-like features take every size and position: an overcomplete set, with no inverse, for detection.
:::

---

**Q7.** In a box feature stack, why does the box SD at 16 px cost the same as at 1 px?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Both come from four lookups in the table of $I$ and four in the table of $I^2$, whatever the window size. Computed directly, the 16 px box ($33 \times 33$, 1089 pixels) would read 121 times as many pixels per window as the 1 px box ($3 \times 3$, 9 pixels).
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* An edge feature of two $w \times h$ rectangles (left − right) lies on the ramp $I(x, y) = 3x + 40$. What is its response divided by the area of one rectangle?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The response is $-a w^2 h = -3w^2h$; divided by $wh$: $-3w$, the slope times the distance $w$ between the centres of the two rectangles.
:::
